item.title: Legal expert details what travelers are entitled to after massive East Coast flight cancellations
item.description: Under U.S. law, travelers affected by the severed cable flight disruptions can claim a full cash refund, but rebooking first could void that right.
item.content:encoded:
After a severed fiber optic cable disrupted thousands of flights to and from East Coast airports on Monday, customers are entitled to a full refund under U.S. law, but they also have other options, Eric Napoli, the chief legal officer at AirHelp, told Fox News Digital.

"Under U.S. domestic law on flights, the rules are that you're entitled to a full cash refund," Napoli explained.

"If you are flying to and from Europe and fall under European rules, if the cause of the delay is directly attributable to the airline, then you could be entitled to up to $700. In this case, this is completely outside of the airline's control. This is a tower-to-ground issue, so you don't get any compensation. But what you are entitled to is — if you decide not to take that flight, or whatever flight they give you next — a full cash refund," Napoli said.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed Amtrak for the cancellations, claiming that a construction crew cut the cable. However, the company quickly pushed back.

LAGUARDIA AIRPORT RUNWAY SHUT DOWN AFTER SINKHOLE DISCOVERED DURING ROUTINE MORNING INSPECTION

"This incident occurred on New Jersey Transit property and involved a New Jersey Transit contractor," Amtrak said in a statement.

NJ Transit acknowledged working on the site where the cable was cut, but claimed "the crew was digging approximately 10 feet away from the utility markings."

Because the incident was not caused by any of the airlines, customers traveling to and from Europe are not entitled to a $700 cash payment that European law would entitle them to if the airport caused the delays, Napoli said.

DELTA FLIGHT DIVERTED TWICE AFTER LAVATORY LEAK FLOODS CABIN, LEAVES PASSENGERS STRANDED FOR HOURS

"In this scenario, European law wouldn't say that the airline has to pay compensation because the network connectivity issue was completely outside of the airline's control — as it would be, for example, if a hurricane were flying in. If the aircraft had a technical issue and they weren't able to fix it in time, that's part of the airline's business and operating model, so an airline would have to pay up to $700," he told Fox News Digital.

Customers are entitled to a full cash refund under U.S. law. However, if they take an offer from the airlines to rebook their flights, they lose the option to get a refund, Napoli said.

"Generally what happens is the airline will come to the passenger and say, 'Either we've canceled the flight or we've rescheduled the flight for the next day, and we've put you on another flight.' The passenger then has the option to say, 'Do I want to take the other flight, or do I not want to?' Maybe now there's no reason to go see the game in Philadelphia, so you don't want to be rescheduled. In that case, you get your money back. If you decide to take the flight, then you wouldn't get your money back because you have consumed a service," he explained.

He recommended customers take initiative in receiving their refunds rather than waiting for the airlines to reimburse them.

"Generally, if you don't ask for it, you're not going to get it, so you have to be pretty proactive. Airlines have gotten really good now with offering rescheduled flights in their apps, because a situation like this is also a headache for them. The airlines have to suddenly find all of these people and rebook them. It's Tetris — along with the domino effect of delay after delay. The airlines will try to help, but for other things like getting a food voucher, a taxi, or a hotel, the traveler is going to have to be savvy and proactive," he continued.

"That's where AirHelp comes in and helps. We have lots of information on our website and a 24/7 chat that keeps you updated. We also have an app that can let you know if your flight is delayed or if incoming flights are on time, so you can look at sources like us. When it comes to things like compensation under European laws, airlines don't make it easy for you," Napoli added.

Napoli ultimately counseled travelers to remain savvy and calm.

"Having information beforehand and knowing how to navigate is always best. Be prepared. Things can go wrong, and we get angry and upset. But getting angry at the people at the airport desk doesn't help the situation — it just makes you angrier. It's best to keep calm, talk to people civilly, and hopefully, things will work out," he told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital contacted the Department of Transportation, Amtrak and New Jersey Transit for comment.

item.title: SEC crowd greets Trump with massive cheers ahead of Tennessee-Texas showdown
item.description: Trump arrived in Knoxville to a roaring Neyland Stadium crowd as the new-look Air Force One flew over ahead of the No. 14 Vols vs. No. 1 Texas kickoff.
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump has arrived in Tennessee for the biggest college football game of the day, and — to the surprise of approximately nobody — the Neyland Stadium crowd went nuts as Air Force I flew over the stadium.

The president arrived in Knoxville about 40 minutes before kickoff of today's marquee showdown between the Vols and No. 1 Texas. It's the first meeting between the two schools since the Cotton Bowl in 1969. Tennessee comes in ranked 14th in the country, while the Longhorns are No. 1 and two weeks removed from an upset of Ohio State.

That was in Austin, though. Today's game is in Knoxville, with the eyes of everyone — including the president — on them.

TRUMP TO ATTEND TEXAS VS TENNESSEE IN HIGH-STAKES COLLEGE FOOTBALL SHOWDOWN

Obviously, it's a very pro-Trump crowd for today's ... SEC ... showdown. Who would've thunk it?! Forget the approval ratings. If Trump goes to an SEC game, he's gonna be cheered. Heavily.

Oddly enough, the only place he may have been met with some boos would've been Austin. Look at what the College GameDay crowd did to Ted Cruz two weeks ago.

TENNESSEE FANS EXCITED FOR TRUMP'S ATTENDANCE AT GAME VS TEXAS: 'I HOPE HE STAYS THE WHOLE GAME'

It was brutal.

But Knoxville is different. Tennessee is a different animal. Fans were told to get to the stadium hours before today's noon kickoff due to heightened security, and they listened.

OutKick's Trey Wallace reports seats were nearly full at the time Trump arrived, which also shouldn't surprise anyone given the school ran a nifty little promotion to entice the masses ...

All drinks, including beer, which half-price between 9 a.m and 10 a.m. That's right. You read that right. Half-price beer at 9 a.m., for a college football game at noon? What could go wrong!

Seems like everyone listened. And for those who did, they were treated to quite the show from Air Force I.

item.title: Bill Maher credits Trump’s ‘kick a--’ crime approach as violent offenses fall across America
item.description: Bill Maher praised Donald Trump's tough-on-crime persona on "Real Time," saying the "f---around-and-find-out president" sent a message to bad guys.
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Bill Maher offered surprising praise for President Donald Trump's handling of crime Friday, telling his audience that the president's tough-guy persona may have played a role in a nationwide drop in violent crime.

"It's not just drug crime that's way down, it's all crime," Maher said during Friday’s episode of HBO’s "Real Time," adding, "And again, probably much of it is not political. It's because you can't move two inches in America without being tracked, photographed, and followed by a Flock camera."

According to the late-night host, the president is a "bad a--" and it's childish to pretend" his tough on crime stance isn't having an impact. 

Maher went on to credit both Democratic policies and Trump with contributing to lower nationwide crime rates.

MAHER MOCKS LIBERALS FOR STILL PANICKING ABOUT TRUMP'S ANTICS, PERSONALITY AFTER 10 YEARS

"It's also because when Democrats expand the safety net, there are less desperate people," Maher said. "And because Trump is a bad a--."

Maher added that while he does not "agree with many of [Trump’s] methods," he cannot argue that the president’s tough-on-crime approach has yielded successful results.

TRUMP TO RALLY WITH NEW YORK POLICE IN HIGHLIGHTING HISTORIC COAST-TO-COAST VIOLENT CRIME DROP

"Is doing it this way the right thing? No. But it's just childish to pretend that when you elect a f---around-and-find-out president, a no-more-Mr.-Nice-Guy, boot-in-your-a--, ‘V for Vendetta,’ kick-a-- and take names, say-hello-to-my-little-friend president, that's not going to have some effect on crime," he continued.

"He has UFC fights on the lawn," Maher concluded. "I think the bad guys got the message."

KASH PATEL TO TOUT 'LARGEST' YEAR-TO-YEAR VIOLENT CRIME DROP IN US HISTORY

According to the FBI’s Crime Data Explorer, reported violent crime nationwide fell 9% from June 2025 through May 2026. Robbery saw the steepest drop, at 19.4%, followed by murder at 18.7%, rape at 10% and aggravated assault at 6.2%.

Retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent Jason Pack also pointed to the potential for bipartisan agreement on crime, telling Fox News Digital that "people may have strong disagreements with other parts of an agenda," but that "there can still be common ground around getting violent offenders off the street and making neighborhoods safer."

CRIME IS FALLING, OFFICIALS SAY — VICTIMS CLAIM REPORTING ISN’T WORTH IT

"You don’t have to wear somebody’s campaign button to admit when something appears to be working. That’s probably why you’re hearing even some of the president’s critics acknowledge what they’re seeing on crime," Pack said.

He emphasized the need for collaboration among local, state and federal law enforcement to make a meaningful difference in fighting crime across the country.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"People can and do disagree about politics. That’s nothing new. But most folks want the same things when they get home at the end of the day," Pack said, adding, "We may never get all the way back to the days when people left the front door unlocked, but folks ought to be able to feel secure in their own neighborhood and know violent offenders are being taken off the street. That’s not red or blue. It seems to me that’s red, white and blue."

The White House also praised the decline in crime, pointing to the statistics in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"President Trump promised to make America safe again and the data proves he has done just that. He has delivered the largest decrease in violent crime in American history," a White House spokesperson said. "Unlike Defund-the-Police Democrats, President Trump will always stand with our law enforcement officers and deliver safer American neighborhoods."

item.title: US, China strike deal to lower tariffs on $30B in goods after Trump-Xi Washington summit
item.description: The United States and China agreed to slash tariffs on $30 billion in goods after Trump and Xi Jinping's three-day Washington summit this week.
item.content:encoded:
The United States and China agreed to lower tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods traded between the two countries following a three-day summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C.

According to the White House, the $30 billion in reciprocal tariff reductions apply to "non-sensitive goods."

U.S. exports including agricultural products, fish and seafood, logs and wood products, cosmetics and medical devices will receive favorable tariff treatment in China. Meanwhile, U.S. imports of Chinese-made small appliances, toys, holiday decorations and children's car seats will also receive preferential treatment.

The agreement was reached through the U.S.-China Board of Trade, a body first proposed during Trump's visit to China in May and formally established during Xi's visit to Washington this week.

XI PRAISES US STATE VISIT 'PERFECTION' AS TRUMP CALLS MEETINGS 'VERY PRODUCTIVE'

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that "a lot more details" about the new trade agreement will be released on Monday.

Greer said the tariff terms were hammered out after weeks of negotiations. Neither country has released the final tariff rates or all the products that will receive favored status going forward.

This marks one of the most significant cooldowns in the trade war Trump launched against China in February 2025, when he levied a 10% tariff on all Chinese imports, citing Beijing's alleged role in the fentanyl crisis and illegal immigration. China hit back with levies on U.S. coal, liquefied natural gas, crude oil and cars.

BESSENT REVEALS EXTENSION TO BUSAN AGREEMENT WITH CHINA UNTIL JANUARY

At their peak, U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods reached a staggering 145% in April 2025, shortly after Trump unveiled his "Liberation Day" reciprocal tariffs. China responded with tariffs of up to 125% on U.S. goods.

U.S. and Chinese negotiators met in Geneva in May 2025 and agreed to a 90-day truce that lowered U.S. tariffs to 30% and China's to 10%. The agreement was extended for another 90 days in August.

Trump and Xi reached another tentative agreement during talks in South Korea in October 2025. Under the deal, China agreed to crack down on fentanyl precursors, resume purchases of U.S. soybeans and ease restrictions on rare-earth exports, while the United States agreed to further ease tariffs.

The two countries will now use the Board of Trade to negotiate additional tariff reductions and other trade disputes, leaving open the possibility of broader agreements in the months ahead.

item.title: Craig Carton calls out Pablo Torre for tying Tim Tebow to alleged Life Surge scam: 'Shame on you'
item.description: Craig Carton slammed Pablo Torre for dragging Tim Tebow into his Life Surge investigative report, saying the report could be actionable defamation.
item.content:encoded:
Craig Carton called out investigative reporter Pablo Torre for his focus on Tim Tebow in a recent report on Life Surge.

Torre alleged that the Christian-focused organization used Tebow as part of a predatory business model that pressured people to hand over thousands of dollars for advice without seeing a return on their investment.

Carton called Torre a "brilliant investigative reporter" but criticized him for linking Tebow to the organization’s alleged conduct without establishing that Tebow knew about it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Tim Tebow doesn't deserve to be dragged into this unless you got him nailed. And if you don't have him nailed to the cross on this story, you have defamed him. And if I'm Tim Tebow, I find that to be actionable. I find that to be regrettable," Carton said on a recent episode of OutKick’s "The Craig Carton Show."

Tebow has since come out and said he is "pausing" his relationship with Life Surge.

"I think the allegations are extremely, extremely serious, and it’s something that we take very serious," Tebow told The Gainesville Sun. "And so, for us, we’re having our team do an investigation, but also pausing our relationship until we can learn more about the facts to be able to understand more."

Mother Jones, which collaborated with Torre on the investigation, reported that Tebow spoke at 20 Life Surge events between 2024 and 2025 and was slated to speak at about as many events in 2026. Carton took no issue with Torre’s investigation but lambasted Torre for what the longtime radio host characterized as using Tebow’s name to further his own career.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"You’re using Tim Tebow’s name and popularity to further your own career. You’re using Tim Tebow to get attention for your story. Whether that story is accurate or not, I’ll take the leap of faith that you’ve reported as an allegation about this Life Surge company that it might even be accurate and factual, and we need to get involved. We need to get district attorneys involved and do a thorough, real investigation to see if they’re committing some type of predatory fraud against honest, God-fearing, blue-collar people who might be losing their life savings under the guise of religion," Carton said.

"That would be awful if that's happening. But how dare you sully the name and reputation of a man who has only done things for others? A man that has dedicated his life to service of his Lord."

Carton criticized Torre for putting Tebow in a bad spot when his reporting did not establish that the Florida Gators legend knew about or participated in the alleged conduct. Carton argued that the report forced Tebow to put out a statement and damaged his public reputation.

"When you go down that road and you sully the reputation of somebody who's dedicated his entire life to service, that is a slippery slope that I want no part of," Carton said.

"So, you better have this locked down, Pablo, and maybe you do, but to throw out an allegation, attach a dude's name to it? Shame on you."

item.title: Scientists reveal surprisingly easy exercise that may boost your mood in just 10 minutes
item.description: A University of Tsukuba study found that a slow 10-minute jog boosted attention, self-control and mood in young adults by activating the prefrontal cortex.
item.content:encoded:
It might not take an all-out sprint or long trail run to lift your mood and sharpen focus, according to a new study.

A small new study out of the University of Tsukuba in Japan looked at 24 healthy young adults who completed a slow, 10-minute run on the treadmill in one session and rested in another.

After the easy jog, participants performed faster on a test of attention and self-control and reported feeling more alert and pleasant than they did after the resting phase, according to the study, which was published in the journal Imaging Neuroscience in August.

'PERFECT' WORKOUT FORMULA CAN TAKE JUST 10 MINUTES A DAY, HILARIA BALDWIN SAYS

Brain monitoring after the jog also showed more activity in parts of the prefrontal cortex, the area of the brain responsible for focus and decision-making.

The jog was purposely kept easy, with participants going at speeds from 1.9 to 3.7 mph on the treadmill. Their average heart rates clocked in at 105 to 107 beats per minute.

SIMPLE BODY MOVEMENT COULD HELP THE BRAIN 'CLEAN ITSELF,' RESEARCHERS FIND

"A single bout of running, even at very slow speed, elicits a pleasant mood and improved executive function," the researchers found.

They added that the finding "sheds light on the slow running benefits to brain health."

JUST 10 MINUTES OF DAILY FLOOR EXERCISES MAY IMPROVE BALANCE AND AGILITY, STUDY FINDS

The benefits, they noted, stuck around even after participants' heart rates returned to baseline.

The greater the up-and-down head movement during the jog, the more positive participants' mood was afterward, though that finding was exploratory and does not necessarily prove cause and effect.

5 COMMON WALKING MISTAKES THAT COULD HURT YOUR PROGRESS, ACCORDING TO AN EXPERT

"Easy movement triggers the norepinephrine and dopamine pathways that wake up the part of the brain that is in charge of focus and self-control," explained Dr. John La Puma, a California-based internist and author of "Indoor Epidemic," who was not involved in the study.

Experts agree, however, that it does not mean one brief workout could be a cure-all.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"A brief jog should help someone get some energy in their system, which may make them feel better about themselves mentally and help them focus," said Dr. Scott Nass, a California-based family medicine physician at SwiftCareMD.

But Nass, who also wasn't involved in the research, said that the effect is likely temporary.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

For people living with depression or anxiety, a jog may briefly clear the mind but is "no substitute for medical care," he told Fox News Digital.

The study was also limited in that it included just 24 healthy, young adults and measured outcomes immediately after just one exercise session. The findings cannot be assumed to apply to older adults, novice runners or people with health conditions and larger studies are needed to confirm the results, Nass said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For a practical approach, La Puma suggested taking a 10-minute walk outside before the most mentally demanding part of the day. Add 30-second jogging intervals, keeping the pace easy enough to speak in full sentences without becoming breathless, he said.

People with heart disease, high blood pressure, Type 1 diabetes, recent surgery or joint pain should check with a clinician before starting a new routine, La Puma advised.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the researchers for comment.

item.title: 'Mike & Molly' star Billy Gardell admits weight loss surgery 'probably saved' his life
item.description: Billy Gardell says bariatric surgery "probably saved my life" after type 2 diabetes and heart concerns forced him to make a drastic decision.
item.content:encoded:
"Mike & Molly" star Billy Gardell is sharing how his dramatic weight loss following his bariatric surgery in 2021 has changed his life.

During a recent appearance on the "Breaking Bread" podcast, the 57-year-old actor said his decision to undergo the surgery "probably saved my life" and described the circumstances which led to him deciding that was the right route for him.

He explained that he had developed type 2 diabetes, as well as "some cholesterol stuff, some heart stuff," joking that his doctor told him that "after 50 the warranties start running out."

"You can't outrun those. I think the only reason I was able to survive as long as I did is one, I got decent genetics, and two was I played some sports when I was younger. So I was a big fat guy, but I was a pretty solid fat guy, and I could carry the weight for a long time, but eventually you can't outrun that."

'REMEMBER THE TITANS' STAR ETHAN SUPLEE SAYS ONE HARD TRUTH FUELED HIS 300-POUND WEIGHT LOSS

After a certain point, Gardell said his doctor approached him and said, "You have to do something."

"I got to the point where I hurt my knee and I couldn't even walk for exercise, and I was like, I have to do something drastic," he said. "So I got the surgery, and it's been a couple years now and I probably saved my life. I'm not on any medication. Diabetes is gone."

Five years after the surgery, the actor explained he has "to be real selective" about what he eats, because he only has "12 ounces to work with," but said the issue with that is "the fat Hulk is still running around" in his mind wanting to overindulge.

Aside from saving his life, the surgery and resulting weight loss also allowed him to do things he couldn't do before, including hiking with his wife and buying something "off the rack" when shopping at the mall.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"It's just those little freedoms that you go, 'Wow, man. I'm so grateful I can do this now,'" he said. "I know those are simple, stupid things, but they mean the world to me."

Gardell explained he decided to get healthy not only for himself, but also for his wife, Patty Knight and their son, William, calling them "my motivating factors."

"It was like I don't want to survive what I've survived, succeed where I succeeded, and then not be able to get out of a chair. So I had to look that in its face. And for anybody out there struggling, if I can do it, you can do it. And don't let nobody tell you different. Do whatever it takes."

Throughout his life, Gardell said he would often fluctuate, losing and gaining 30 pounds every year, noting at his heaviest, he weighed 379 pounds.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

During an interview with People in December 2025, the actor said he now maintains his weight through diet and exercise, noting, "I fluctuate between 210 and 215" pounds.

Gardell rose to fame on the hit sitcom "Mike & Molly," playing Melissa McCarthy's husband on the show for six seasons from 2010 to 2016.

item.title: Tennessee fans excited for Trump's attendance at game vs Texas: 'I hope he stays the whole game'
item.description: Neyland Stadium opened its gates early with 50% off beer as Tennessee Vols fans gear up for the No. 1 Texas SEC showdown and Trump's arrival.
item.content:encoded:
The gates at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville were open at 9 a.m., alcoholic beverages were 50% off, and the vibes amongst Tennessee Volunteers fans were extremely high as their SEC matchup against No. 1 Texas comes with the arrival of President Donald Trump.

While there are heightened security protocols, road closures and more that will surely cause some delays compared to a normal gameday on campus, Vols fans were able to enter Neyland Stadium at 9 a.m., allowing them more than ample time to get into the stadium before 12 p.m. ET kick-off.

And as an incentive to get fans in the doors, Neyland Stadium offered 50% beers between 9-10 a.m. Only two were allowed at each purchase, but you were allowed to come back as many times as you wanted within that hour for the special deal.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But while Vols fans are already enjoying this deal, they’re more excited for the 47th president traveling to watch a premier college football matchup that will occur for only the fifth time in each team’s history.

"Glad he’s here. I hope he stays the whole game, we’ll see how it goes. Go Vols!" one fan told OutKick’s Trey Wallace after he and two friends took advantage of the 50% off alcohol sale at the concession stands.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"[It will be a] great time and enjoy it. Glad he’s here," another Vols fan said.

Another added: "MAGA, go Trump, baby. Let’s go!"

The hype surrounding this game was large well before Trump announced his expected attendance. Texas gained top-team status in the AP poll after a thrilling second-half comeback against Ohio State, the previous No. 1 team in the country, two weeks ago. They have the targets on their back now, and they enter a hostile Neyland Stadium environment where Tennessee, the 14th-ranked team in the country, is hoping to upset them at home.

Led by freshman quarterback Faizon Brandon, the Vols possess a tremendous offense and could use their home crowd like Texas did in Austin against the Buckeyes to remain undefeated and pick up a great SEC victory.

Of course, those Vols fans who spoke to Wallace believe that will be the case. Their final score predictions, though, might be a little hard to believe.

"67-0," one said before his friend added, "68-0." Then, a more reasonable score was put out there.

item.title: Oxford mayor warns kratom is 'rolling the dice on death' as fears linger over Ole Miss deaths
item.description: Oxford Mayor Robyn Tannehill warns kratom is "rolling the dice on death" after two Ole Miss student deaths rattled the Mississippi campus.
item.content:encoded:
Oxford, Mississippi, Mayor Robyn Tannehill issued a stark warning Saturday about the dangers of kratom and other "gas station drugs" after packaged kratom was recovered during investigations into the deaths of two Ole Miss students.

"To take kratom is really rolling the dice on death..." Tannehill told "Fox & Friends Weekend."

"So our challenge right now is to make our young people understand the dangers of these drugs."

TWO OLE MISS STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS PACKAGED KRATOM IS RECOVERED AT TWO SITES: OFFICIALS

Tannehill said Oxford's city board passed a law prohibiting the sale of kratom at gas stations seven years ago, and that local authorities have been aware of the substance's dangers for some time.

"This is a substance that our police chief identified as dangerous in 2019, and we immediately took action," she said.

"So these investigations are ongoing. We are always trying to find the bad actors in our community that are choosing to sell these things to kids."

The two students were found dead Monday, Sept. 21, in separate locations — one on campus and the other off campus. Although their causes of death remain undetermined, narcotics detectives are involved in both investigations.

Authorities say, if the reports find fentanyl, a special Mississippi law can be used to target the seller.

THE FRAT OMERTÀ: WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS OF ‘CODE OF SILENCE’ AFTER OLE MISS DEATHS, ALLEGED PENN STATE COKE RING

The news has triggered fears among many Ole Miss students. One student, speaking on "The Faulkner Focus" Thursday, said some students are cautious of what they eat or drink as fears mount on campus.

Tannehill, however, attempted to assuage some of those fears.

"Oxford is an extremely safe town," she said.

"It's a place that, when you walk down the street, people still speak to you," she added. "It's a place that takes care of each other... the issues that we're dealing with right now are the issues that every college campus across the nation is dealing with. It's not unique to Oxford. Unfortunately, the spotlight is on Oxford now because of these two tragic deaths and, if that spotlight can help us save other kids, then my prayer is that this makes somebody check up and say, 'You know what, I'm not going to do that [try any substances].'"

Tannehill also reiterated that the Oxford community is awaiting autopsy and toxicology reports and until those tests are in, many details are speculation. Reports are expected to be completed as early as next week, according to the state's commissioner of public safety.

Oxford police have separately announced arrests in connection with a raid on a tobacco shop accused of trafficking narcotics.

Authorities have identified 18-year-old Aidan Hamilton and 20-year-old Robert Strang as the victims.

Fox News' Adam Sabes, Michael Ruiz and Madison Scarpino contributed to this report.

item.title: Will Tennessee zoom past No. 1 Texas? These Vols competing in auto innovation have already hit the gas
item.description: University of Tennessee engineering students are transforming a Jeep Grand Cherokee with self-driving capabilities in the 2026 EcoCAR Innovation Challenge.
item.content:encoded:
Speed. Strength. Smarts. Efficiency.

All things that have been top of mind in Knoxville this week. And not just for the University of Tennessee football team.

TENNESSEE VOLUNTEERS LOOK TO PROVE PLAYOFF CREDENTIALS AGAINST TOP-RANKED TEXAS LONGHORNS FOOTBALL

As the No. 14 Volunteers prepared for Saturday’s tilt against No. 1 Texas in Knoxville, another group of Tennessee students were putting on their game faces for the challenge of their young lives.

"We’re at the very beginning stages," Tennessee Ph.D. student Tyson Beach said. "Right now, it’s just this big bowl of potential. We are forming ideas, but we are driven, we are working and we want to win. That’s just it. Plain and simple."

Beach and his more than 100 teammates from Tennessee’s Tickle College of Engineering were selected to compete in the 2026 EcoCAR Innovation Challenge against 19 other universities from across North America.

The four-year program, administered by the U.S. Department of Energy and Argonne National Laboratory, and sponsored by car manufacturers General Motors and Stellantis, tasks college students with developing innovative and energy-efficient next-generation solutions for the automotive industry, using emerging technologies, artificial intelligence, connected and automated vehicle systems and advanced propulsion.

DRIVERLESS RACING GOES GLOBAL. WILL FANS CARE?

The Tennessee students, who will be working on transforming a Jeep Grand Cherokee, as some of the other teams work on a Chevrolet Blazer, were in Atlanta this week at a conference to get their marching orders about how the competition works and what they need to do to win the title in 2030.

"There are about 30 deliverables (to Stellantis, the manufacturer of Jeep) on our dashboard in just this year), which means our students will be working day and night, battling to get this job done," said Pingen Chen, the team’s sponsor and a professor in the mechanical and aerospace engineering department at Tennessee. "It’s a lot of time management, collaborations, teamwork and coming up with ideas. It’s a great collaborative platform."

WOULD YOU RIDE IN WAYMO'S NEW OJAI ROBOTAXI?

The Tennessee students already have a game plan in mind. Not only are they tasked by Stellantis to optimize the Grand Cherokee’s off-road capabilities, they are determined to set themselves apart by adding their own creative innovations that will enhance self-driving capabilities on the vehicle.

"We will follow the specific requirements, but then we want to go above and beyond, and I think we can do that by providing something related to autonomy," Tennessee Ph.D. student Skylar Sims said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

While Sims and his teammates acknowledge that the general public might still be skeptical about self-driving cars, they say they are committed to mainstreaming that feature by developing more consistent technology.

"You know, when cars first came out, people would say, ‘I don’t trust driving a car. I have a horse, let me ride my horse,’" Sims said with a smile. "When anything new comes out, there’s skepticism. It just takes time to implement and improve and gain people’s trust to make it more safe. I’ve worked over the past two years on autonomous vehicles, so I’m excited about that."

The Tennessee team is also excited about its potential, and its talent and its versatility. The students believe they have a great chance to win another title, which would bookend a championship by Tennessee in the very first EcoCAR Challenge back in 1988.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

"I think we have a deep history (in the competition)," Tennessee Ph.D. student Zakerie Hubbs said. "And we’re a large university with a lot of resources. And we have a passion in the group, especially with autonomous vehicles.

"There’s pressure to it because it’s a competition, but that adds an exhilaration to it too. We’re really excited to be here, and we think we’re going to have a lot of fun."

Will Tennessee defeat No. 1 Texas today? Will the Vols win the EcoCAR Challenge in 2030? Let me know your predictions: patricia.babcockmcgraw@outkick.com

item.title: Curt Cignetti drops insane "Pearl Harbor" line after Indiana squeaks by Northwestern
item.description: Curt Cignetti said Indiana got "Pearl Harbored" after back-to-back false starts and a goal line turnover opened an ugly 29-23 Big Ten victory.
item.content:encoded:
Defending champion Indiana survived a scare Friday night against Northwestern, eking out a 29-23 win in the 2026 Big Ten opener.

The Hoosiers were nearly three touchdown favorites most of the week, but that never came close to hitting. In fact, for most of the first quarter, Indiana led Northwestern by a robust score of ...

2-0.

INDIANA QB JOSH HOOVER DELIVERS THE GREATEST 'FOOTBALL GUY' MOMENT OF THE SEASON SO FAR

That's right. 2-0! Nothing like a little Friday night pitcher's duel in Bloomington. It's rare to see a 2-0 score in a football game, by the way. Duh.

So when it happens, you have to soak it in.

Amazing. I could watch it all day. Again, you just don't see it. Old school football, baby!

Anyway, it was a struggle for Indiana most of the night. The Hoosiers had leads of 2-0, 5-0, 12-0, and 12-7 before Northwestern closed the gap to 22-20 midway through the fourth quarter.

The defending champs prevailed, but it wasn't pretty. Perhaps opening the game with back-to-back false starts — followed by a turnover on downs at the goal line — was a harbinger of things to come.

At least that's what head coach Curt Cignetti took away ...

Sort of:

"We got Pearl Harbored the first two offensive plays."

Well, that's certainly one way to put it. I'll be honest, I've never heard that one. Good stuff here from Cignetti. Nobody does it quite like him.

The guy is just a content machine. It's Cignetti, Lane Kiffin, and then everyone else.

Cig has owned college football for the better part of a year now. He came into Indiana, made the Hoosiers a football school, led them to a national title and he doesn't appear to be slowing down this season.

COCKY CURT CIGNETTI CALLED OUT THE SEC, BUT HE SHOULD GOOGLE INDIANA'S LAUGHABLE SCHEDULE FIRST

Magical quotes like this, of course, are a dime a dozen from Cignetti. Remember, this is the guy who started his tenure at Indiana by telling a group of reporters to "Google me."

We mocked him them. Nobody's laughing now.

The Hoosiers are sort of coasting their way through the first part of the season. Not a ton of folks talking about them.

But the schedule goes up a notch in October with Michigan and Ohio State looming.

Cignetti said it best last night.

There's a war brewing.

item.title: Florida real estate sees surge from Washington high earners fleeing new millionaire income tax
item.description: Pacific Northwest millionaires are buying Florida real estate as Washington state's looming 9.9% income tax hike pushes high-net-worth individuals south.
item.content:encoded:
Washington state millionaires are increasingly eyeing Florida real estate to escape a changing tax landscape in the Pacific Northwest, according to a luxury real estate expert.

"I would say that the first thing is taxes. Income tax in Florida is 0%, and in Washington state, it's 9.9% as of January 2028," Margit Brandt, a luxury property specialist, told Fox News Digital.

"Capital gains in Florida is also 0%, and in Washington state, it's 7%. I just think that they've created this really punitive tax environment that's unappealing to the high-net-worth individuals who are the high earners in Washington State, and that's been the biggest kind of feeder for our market here," she added.

Washington's capital gains tax is tiered, with the first $1 million in taxable Washington capital gains subject to a 7% rate and amounts above $1 million subject to a 9.9% rate. Real estate is exempt from the tax.

TRUCKING COMPANY OWNER SUING STATE OVER 'MILLIONAIRES TAX' SAYS POLICY HITS SMALL BUSINESSES

The push comes after the Democratic-controlled Washington Legislature passed, and Gov. Bob Ferguson signed, a 9.9% levy on annual adjusted gross income above the law's $1 million threshold. Set to take effect on Jan. 1, 2028 — with initial returns due in April 2029 — the legislation marks a major change for a state that currently has no individual income tax.

The tax is already facing a court challenge over its constitutionality, while real estate insiders say the new law is influencing some wealthy residents' relocation decisions.

SEATTLE MAYOR SHRUGS OFF MILLIONAIRE-TAX CONCERNS AS 44% OF BUSINESS LEADERS CONSIDER LEAVING

"We've seen actual deals — big deals — happen with high earners from Washington state," Brandt said. "This is not hypothetical. These are closed transactions with people setting up a whole new life here in Florida."

While comprehensive data tracking millionaire migration following the new tax are not yet available, a recent business survey found increased interest among respondents in relocating.

A recent survey released by the Association of Washington Business (AWB) — the state's chamber of commerce and manufacturers association — found that 24% of respondents said they were considering moving their businesses out of Washington. That figure is up from 17% in the previous quarter and nearly triple the rate recorded 16 months ago. 

Furthermore, 55% of surveyed business leaders said they are considering moving their personal residence to another state — a number that climbs to 67% in Spokane County, near the low-tax Idaho border.

WHY STARBUCKS PICKED NASHVILLE OVER SEATTLE FOR EXPANSION, ACCORDING TO LOCAL BUSINESS REPORTER

The shift is mirrored in high-profile individual departures. Jesse Proudman, founder and CTO of privacy-focused AI platform Venice.ai, told Fox News Digital in May that he was leaving the Evergreen State, warning that a region once known as a "startup sanctuary" has grown increasingly hostile to business leaders.

Similarly, coffee giant Starbucks announced in April that it would invest $100 million to set up an additional support office in Nashville, Tennessee — a state with no individual income tax — where it expects to have 2,000 support jobs over the next five years. Starbucks said those jobs will include newly created positions, work brought in-house and some teams moved from Seattle.

Beyond balance sheets, Brandt said that safety, culture, and quality of life are primary drivers for wealthy transplants moving to Florida and other states, including Texas and the Carolinas.

"If they're looking at a $10 million house, a $20 million house, a $50 million house, or a $100 million house, it's more than just a house. It's a whole new lifestyle," Brandt said, adding that Florida’s lack of a state estate tax and its proximity to the Caribbean appeal heavily to multi-generational wealth. "They want safety, security, good schools, and to set up their financial future. Florida is just such an easy landing place, and I think we're going to see way more of it in the coming years."

A spokesperson for Senator Patty Murray, D-Wash, told Fox News Digital: "This is an issue subject to initiative, currently on the ballot in our state. For that reason, I’m limited in what I can say on the issue." 

Fox News Digital also reached out to Senator Maria Cantwell, D-Wash, as well as Washington state’s governor, Bob Ferguson. 

Fox News Digital also reached out to State Sen. Jamie Pedersen (D-Seattle), the architect of the millionaire's tax bill, for comment and to Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson.

item.content:encoded:

Anyone? Any takers? Bueller?

... Bueller?!

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

That's right. Tickets for an actual NFL game — a New York Giants game, no less — are going for a pound of ground beef at Publix.

Grass-fed only, of course. MAHA!

Take a look:

The problem, I'd imagine, will be getting to the actual stadium. Who knows what that commute's gonna look like Sunday morning. The northeast is set to get dumped on all weekend as this storm bears down. I've lived through dozens of hurricanes. I've lived through several nor'easters. Both are terrible. You never know what you're gonna wake up to in the morning.

GIANTS' JAXSON DART TRIED TO REENTER GAME WITH KNEE INJURY BUT HAD JERSEY TAKEN AWAY: REPORTS

That being said ... I'd imagine the loss of Jaxson Dart isn't helping ticket sales, either. Dart, the Giants' star quarterback, took a nasty hit to the knee last Monday night in Los Angeles, and underwent season-ending surgery earlier this week.

Jameis Winston is set to take over full-time starting duties under center for John Harbaugh for the rest of the year, and Winston didn't exactly light it up in relief in Monday's loss.

GIANTS 'HATE' THEIR FANS AFTER HOW THEY HANDLED JAXSON DART'S SEASON-ENDING INJURY, CRAIG CARTON SAYS

So, yeah ... you add it all up — the weather, the injury to Dart, the opposition — and it turns up a $14 ticket in the nosebleeds.

So ... any takers?

item.title: Record WNBA viewership proves the league's drama is driving fans to screens, not away from them | Matt Calkins
item.description: WNBA ratings hit a record 1.37 million viewers this season as drama involving Caitlin Clark and league controversies fuel unprecedented attention.
item.content:encoded:
You're bored, and you want to convince your WNBA-loving friend that the league is a disaster. So you put together a list. 

You write down how the league's most popular player, Caitlin Clark, had her throat pushed in by Alyssa Thomas, but needed NBA Commissioner Adam Silver to step in and get Thomas suspended. You add how Caitlin is constantly left out of marketing campaigns, and was voted the 11th best guard in the WNBA by her peers.

You throw in how the league's leaders still can't define what a woman is despite having a meeting on the subject. You jot down that teams regularly ban media (see: OutKick) they suspect will ask unflattering questions. You conclude with commissioner Cathy Engelbert once dismissing a fair question about her future by saying "I wonder whether you would ask that of a man," then note that she will retire after 2026.

CAITLIN CLARK HELPS FEVER DELIVER WNBA'S LARGEST REGULAR-SEASON TV AUDIENCE IN 29 YEARS

You give the list to your buddy. He just smiles.

Check the TV ratings and attendance figures, he says.

Shoot. He might just have you.

Folks can complain about the WNBA being a circus all they want, but circuses tend to draw a lot of people into the tent. One could argue that the league has done a number on its reputation, but you can't argue with the number of eyeballs watching its teams.

The WNBA averaged a record 1.37 million viewers across the ESPN networks during this regular season, which marked a 17% increase from last year. NBC and CBS also averaged at least one million viewers for their WNBA packages in 2026.

And it's not just the broadcasts luring in fans. The league drew a record 3.79 million live attendees across 330 games, which is a 20.5% increase from last season. Yes, the two expansion teams inflated these numbers, but the average WNBA attendance of 11,474 was still a 5% increase from last regular season.

How much of this is cash cow Caitlin Clark being healthy after missing most of last season?

That certainly helps, but this goes beyond CC. Games not involving the Fever averaged 984,000 viewers this regular season — up 24% from last year.

You can't tell me that isn't significant. You can't look at those numbers and say the WNBA is self-destructing.

Perhaps one could argue that viewership and attendance would be even higher if smarter leadership kept the controversies at bay. But maybe, just maybe — the controversies are what's behind this boost.

WILL THE WNBA’S UNSERIOUS, WEEKLY SITCOM DESTROY ONE OF THE GREATEST OPPORTUNITIES FOR WOMEN ATHLETES?

As much as tradition and physical excellence drive sports viewership, drama is every bit as crucial. And whether it's the players' contempt for Clark, Sophie Cunningham's pointing meme, or the league's genuflection to trans activists —theater has the WNBA in the news every day.

I once described it as half basketball, half WWE. My dad corrected me on that — it's half basketball, half Real Housewives of Hoop.

When Clark barks at refs, or yells at White, or gets chewed out by Fever assistant coach Briann January — we don't turn away. Fans condemn players such as Thomas or Chennedy Carter or Mabrey for malicious fouls on Caitlin, but they don't skip the next game.

Natasha Cloud losing her mind on Enes Kanter for wearing a shirt with the definition of a woman on it? Absurd. But it was a talker for a good week. Coach after coach giving pro trans answers when asked about the separation of biological men and women? Predictable, but incessantly newsworthy. The maligning of Fever supporters as racist middle Americans invading the league? Infuriating. But while fans roll their eyes one second, they glue them to the TV the next.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

I'll admit I'm as guilty as anyone. In addition to everything above, the WNBA's cowardice in banning media makes me want to stage a personal boycott. And yet, when the Fever start their playoff series against the Aces Sunday, I'll be as invested in that as any NFL game.

There's a lot of talk about how the actions of players, coaches and leaders prevent the WNBA from being taken seriously. But part of me wonders if most of them even care about being taken seriously.

They have their money. They have their eyeballs. They have their culture. Respect from the everyman may be immaterial to them.

Like any reality show, the Real Housewives of Hoop will leave you teeming with anger and frustration. But you can't help but tune into the next episode.

item.title: Damaged fragment deemed 'unremarkable' turns out to be rare piece of Homer's 'Odyssey' history
item.description: A fragment of Homer's "Odyssey" Book 12 sat unnoticed for decades in Utrecht University's archives until a Radboud University professor recognized it.
item.content:encoded:
An ancient fragment of Homer's "Odyssey" was hiding in plain sight for decades in a university library in the Netherlands — until a professor took a closer look.

The discovery, announced by Utrecht University this month, was made in the university's Special Collections.

Mark de Kreij, an assistant professor of Ancient Greek and Papyrology at Radboud University, came across the unidentified parchment while studying Greek manuscripts in the university's collection.

EXPERTS STUNNED AFTER UNCOVERING HOMER'S 'ILIAD' ON EGYPTIAN MUMMY IN UNPRECEDENTED FIND

De Kreij told Fox News Digital the fragment had originally been kept with Coptic Christian manuscripts, which he said was "probably why it was missed in the early research on the collection."

By the time he examined it, however, the still-unidentified fragment had been moved to a box containing Greek manuscripts.

Utrecht University said the fragment was first considered ordinary.

"Hidden among these, first regarded as an unremarkable 7th-century fragment, was a damaged and discolored fragment with very small, neat letters," the university said.

"De Kreij soon recognized a few words typical of the Homeric epics."

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER 1,700-YEAR-OLD CHRISTIAN CITY HIDDEN BENEATH EGYPT'S DESERT

The fragment contains verses from Book 12 of the "Odyssey" — including the pivotal moment when the sun god Helios discovers that Odysseus' crew killed and ate his sacred cattle.

Helios then demands vengeance from Zeus — an episode recently depicted in the Christopher Nolan film adaptation.

Researchers believe the manuscript was owned by a reader living in Egypt's Fayum oasis, southwest of modern-day Cairo, around 300 A.D. 

The fragment has been dated to the 3rd or 4th century A.D.

And its age isn't the only thing that makes it a rarity. The university says only a few fragments like it exist across the world.

ONE OF HISTORY'S MOST FAMOUS BATTLES COULD BE REWRITTEN BY LONG-LOST PAPAL LETTER

"There are only around 30 fragments like it worldwide," the statement said.

Though the university described the fragment as part of a "pocket edition" of the complete epic, one expert told Fox News Digital she was not convinced by that interpretation.

Anna Dolganov, a Roman historian and papyrologist at the Austrian Archaeological Institute of the Austrian Academy of Sciences in Vienna, questioned whether the fragment came from a complete copy of Homer's epic.

"The entire ‘Odyssey’ would require 480 pages," she said.

ANCIENT BOOK OF REVELATION CITY GIVES UP STUNNING SECRET BURIED FOR 1,500 YEARS

Dolganov noted that a parchment volume of that length would be extremely thick in such a small format — making it unlikely, in her view, that the codex contained the entire epic.

The expert also pointed to the handwriting, which she described as more casual and cursive than what she would expect in a complete literary work.

"What I think it's more likely to be is an anthology," she posited. "Or a private collection of excerpts from literary texts, possibly for use in schools, for education, or a private anthology that would have been much, much smaller — not the entire 'Odyssey.'"

De Kreij pointed to the text preserved on both sides of the parchment as evidence that it belonged to a complete copy of the epic.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Both sides contain passages from book 12 of the ‘Odyssey,’ which are nearly contiguous," he told Fox News Digital.

De Kreij said an anthology is theoretically possible, but he knows of no similar examples from the period. Complete copies of works such as the "Iliad" and "Odyssey," by contrast, have numerous parallels, he said.

Dolganov said the discovery also reflects Homer's widespread popularity in the ancient world, where his works played an important role in education.

The ancient poet "was very popular indeed all over the Mediterranean world where Greek was learned," Dolganov said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Homer was used to teach Greek," she added, explaining that his works were widely used as school texts around the Eastern Mediterranean.

Dolganov noted that dating ancient literary manuscripts can be difficult and imprecise, particularly in situations where scholars rely on handwriting as evidence.

"It would be important not to overstate how certain we are that this is indeed as early as the third or fourth century," she said.

"But it doesn't need to be, to be a very interesting and exciting discovery," she said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

De Kreij said the dating is based on several features of the fragment, including its codex format, parchment material, the appearance of the ink and its handwriting.

"The neat, small bookhand cannot be dated with absolute certainty, but there are good parallels from the late third and fourth century," he said.

"All such dating has to be approximate, but in the scientific edition, I cite a number of dated parallels to back up my estimate."

Dolganov also reflected on the human connection offered by the discovery.

"This is something that people held in their hand," she said. "This is something they carried with them and read, and it's a text that's also accessible to us."

"So it kind of connects us to the ancient reader because we are similarly excited by this timeless work of literature."

item.title: 'Betting on Beloit' star Konya Hendricks Schuh reveals bizarre discovery hidden inside wall
item.description: Diane Hendricks' daughter Konya Hendricks Schuh tackles the city's worst houses on A&E's "Betting on Beloit," tearing into neglected homes.
item.content:encoded:
Home design expert Konya Hendricks Schuh has found family history, forgotten memorabilia and plenty of surprises inside Beloit's neglected homes.

But one discovery, she told Fox News Digital, was downright bizarre.

The unexpected twist happened as Schuh's "Betting on Beloit" renovation team — her husband, Matt, and project manager Pete Woodkey — was tearing into a property for Season 2 of the A&E series.

REALITY STAR WARNS AMERICAN FAMILIES ARE BUYING ‘NIGHTMARE HOMES’ THEY CAN’T AFFORD TO FIX

"Oh, the wildest thing, in season two," she began to tell Fox News Digital, "It was just kind of funny. Matt and Pete were demoing a house, and they pulled out … it was more bizarre, definitely not sentimental, but we're in the drywall, ripping drywall off, and there was … ladies' vintage lingerie buried — so they pulled out this little lacy number and that was pretty surprising. That was new."

The stranger discoveries are balanced by pieces of Beloit history, including old newspapers, photographs and boxes of family memorabilia found in an abandoned attic.

WATCH: ‘BETTING ON BELOIT’ STAR DISCOVERS BIZARRE ITEMS BEHIND DEMO WALL DURING HOME RENOVATION

"Whoever lived in that home, they had won a lot of awards … 75 years ago from Beloit Corp. So just kind of rummaging through all of that was a pretty cool experience."

‘GOLD RUSH’ STAR WARNS WASHINGTON HAS ‘ZERO INTEREST’ IN FIXING THE DEBT, FUELING A MASSIVE GOLD BOOM

Schuh and her family aren't simply renovating houses. They're betting on the city itself.

When Fox News Digital asked whether she was trying to rebuild the American dream her family created from scratch for a new generation, Schuh said, "Absolutely."

WATCH: ‘BETTING ON BELOIT’ STAR CONFESSES TO BEING THE SET'S ULTIMATE PERFECTIONIST

"The houses that we buy are truly the worst in the neighborhood. That really is what our mission is… the houses bringing the neighborhood down."

JOANNA GAINES REVEALS WHY SHE AND CHIP WALKED AWAY FROM 'FIXER UPPER' AT THE HEIGHT OF ITS SUCCESS

Schuh is the daughter of billionaire entrepreneur and philanthropist Diane Hendricks, and "Betting on Beloit" puts their family legacy front and center.

Her husband, Matt, works alongside her as a plumbing contractor and former home builder, while her nephew, Connor Fox, is part of the real estate team.

The goal is to make Beloit a place where families want to stay — and where new families want to put down roots.

"We want people … and our talent to stay here in our town and not move away to bigger cities or more metropolitan areas, but then we're also really working hard to attract new talent and new families to Beloit."

WATCH: ‘BETTING ON BELOIT’ STAR RISKS BIG FINANCIAL HIT ON MASSIVE $975K HOME PROJECT

Season 2 also brings bigger financial risks. 

Schuh's largest project to date, a massive Dutch Colonial formerly used as college housing, is listed at $975,000 and remains on the market.

"But I love it, and it was a great house to work on. I'm super proud of it."

For Schuh, that's the bigger bet: turning neglected properties into homes that can become part of someone else's American dream.

"Making these old houses that need serious love, and then we tackle those — we really ultimately try to make them really the prize of the neighborhood and really something to be proud of."

item.title: 'Primetime' Review: Robert Pattinson channels Chris Hansen in riveting dramatization of 'To Catch a Predator'
item.description: Fox News Digital reviews A24's new reality TV thriller "Primetime" starring Robert Pattison, Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo. Directed by Lance Oppenheim.
item.content:encoded:
"Have a seat."

Those words were memorably said by Chris Hansen, the "Dateline NBC" correspondent who hosted the provocative reality series "To Catch a Predator" during the 2000s. 

Hansen, notably, had zero involvement in the making of A24's new film, "Primetime," which was adapted from a 2007 Esquire article titled "Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die." In fact, according to Hansen, the studio wanted him to sign a restrictive agreement before showing him the movie, which he refused to do.

After watching "Primetime," you can see why A24 was hoping for a legal cover. Because unless you're Hansen or any other key people involved, it's difficult to know where the reality ends and where the fiction begins.

‘RESIDENT EVIL’ REVIEW: DIRECTOR ZACH CREGGER DELIVERS INFECTIOUS REBOOT TO GORY VIDEO GAME FRANCHISE

Robert Pattinson steps into the role as Hansen, a self-aggrandizing and rather eccentric journalist eying to be taken seriously by his NBC colleagues — perhaps with the success of "To Catch a Predator."

If you aren't familiar, "To Catch a Predator" exposed men who believed they were meeting minors after sexually explicit online conversations. Instead, they walked into sting operations that typically ended with Hansen emerging from another room to confront them before police made arrests.

The show's producer, Andie Bender (Merritt Wever) is just as essential as its star. Her job is to keep the engine running and to make sure Hansen doesn't drift into a mental abyss. It isn't until she and Hansen are brought into the office of NBC chief Jeff Zucker (humorously played by Zucker himself), who informs them he's moving their show into primetime, giving them the daunting task of going up against ABC juggernaut "LOST" in the same time slot. 

'THE DOG STARS' REVIEW: JACOB ELORDI FIGHTS FOR SURVIVAL IN RIDLEY SCOTT'S DULL POST-APOCALYPTIC WESTERN

In "Primetime," the predators are also the prey as Hansen and his team go to incredible lengths to nab a creep, but more importantly, to make great television. Some members of the team grapple with the ethics and morality of their line of work. Hansen, at least the film's version of him, views himself as a saint, carrying out a righteous mission despite his own shortcomings in his personal life. But it's far more nuanced for new hire Dan Plumb (Skyler Gisondo), a 23-year-old aspiring actor hired to play a 13-year-old decoy. You can tell how visibly shaken he is by the process, and he struggles with whether obtaining the coveted Screen Actors Guild membership card is worth ruining other people's lives for.

BOX OFFICE COMEBACK: HOW SUMMER 2026 OFFERS A GLIMMER OF HOPE FOR HOLLYWOOD IN THE POST-COVID ERA

Pattinson has had an impressive year between "The Drama" and "The Odyssey" (not to mention "Dune: Part Three" in December), proving he's come a long way from his "Twilight" days. He gives a career-best performance as a self-obsessed, borderline unhinged NBC host. While he gets top billing, the emotional crutch of the entire movie rests on Gisondo's shoulders. Best known for his stint on HBO's "The Righteous Gemstones" and more recently playing Jimmy Olsen in the new "Superman" movie, Gisondo is able to show depth from Dan's charming naivety to utter demoralization. Wever also shines as the no-nonsense producer who has to put up with a lot of nonsense.

Director Lance Oppenheim's background in documentaries shows in "Primetime" between the reliance on the hidden cameras that only fuels the intensity and the cutaways to various cultural references. The low-resolution style takes viewers back to a pre-4K era and the shadows provide a noir element.

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

What can be viewed as an indictment of how sleazy the television industry can be, "Primetime" isn't exactly the feel-good movie of the year, but it's a riveting thriller that showcases outstanding performances from Pattinson, Gisondo and Wever.

"Primetime" is rated R for disturbing sexual material, graphic nudity, some violent content, and language. Running time: 1 hour, 50 minutes. In theaters now.

item.title: Hidden California desert pet cemetery holds unexpected piece of White House history
item.description: Charley Stewart's Haven for Pets in Desert Hot Springs holds graves of Gerald Ford's dog Liberty and pets once owned by Liberace and Hollywood stars.
item.content:encoded:
When members of the Secret Service swarmed Charley Stewart’s plot of land in the middle of California's Sonoran Desert, he wasn’t confused or worried — he knew what they had come for.

"They have representatives, the Secret Service, and the secretaries, and all those people come by," he told Fox News Digital. "It’s like a circus."

Stewart owns and operates Haven for Pets, a pet cemetery in Desert Hot Springs. When one of the nation’s most famous dogs — former President Gerald Ford’s golden retriever, Liberty — was set to be buried there, Secret Service agents visited the cemetery to inspect the grounds ahead of the burial, Stewart said.

DISCOVERIES THAT RESHAPED WHAT HISTORIANS KNEW ABOUT AMERICA'S FOUNDING FATHERS

"Before she got buried out there, the Secret Service had to go out and look for mines and walk around," said the cemetery owner. "I mean, Gerald Ford was the President of the United States."

The female golden retriever arrived at the White House as a puppy and became the nation’s first dog, later giving birth to nine puppies in 1975 on the third floor of the White House. 

Liberty was the first dog to give birth in the White House.

The frequently photographed canine enjoyed the White House life. She posed on the North Lawn, lounged beside the commander in chief in the Oval Office, swam in the pool at Camp David and even received fan mail from Americans across the country.

The Fords kept one of Liberty’s puppies, a female named Misty, who is buried alongside her mother at Haven for Pets. Their grave sites leave an unexpected piece of presidential history tucked away in Stewart’s pet cemetery.

RONALD REAGAN'S GRANDDAUGHTER, KEVIN MCCARTHY HONOR LATE PRESIDENT'S LEGACY ON HIS 115TH BIRTHDAY

Stewart’s Haven for Pets dates back to the 1960s. It opened as an extension of a full-service Palm Springs kennel called Dogtown USA, which was known for providing grooming services to celebrity pets.

Dogtown was purchased by Stewart’s father, Charles Stewart, in 1959, and Stewart recalled the story of how the pet cemetery came to be.

"My father told me a story one time — he went over to talk to some people and their dog had died, and they threw it in a garbage can, and the head was hanging out," Stewart said. "From that horrible sight, my father said, ‘We’ve got to take care of these babies.’ And so he decided to do that."

"It took a couple years to do the paperwork, but that’s what he did … This was an input my father never got over," he added.

Haven for Pets’ celebrity canine clientele extends beyond the White House, all the way to Hollywood.

STAGECOACH FESTIVALGOERS SPLIT ON WHETHER AMERICA IS HEADED IN THE RIGHT DIRECTION AHEAD OF ITS 250TH BIRTHDAY

World-famous pianist Liberace has six of his dogs buried in the cemetery, under headstones that list their owner as "Lee," his nickname. Actor Michael Landon and Academy Award-winning composer Jimmy Van Heusen also have their pets buried there.

Stewart told Fox News Digital the VIP connections grew out of his family’s work caring for pets belonging to celebrities who lived in the Coachella Valley.

"Going back to Leonard Firestone and the Marx Brothers down here in Thunderbird Country Club, my dad would take care of their dogs," he shared. "We’d groom them and we boarded them … We did business with them."

Roughly 1,000 pets are buried in the cemetery. In its early days decades ago, the burial rate was $35. These days it costs nearly $900.

Stewart said that, at one point, the cemetery would handle five burials a week, but the figure has fallen to three or four a year because he wants to limit the frequency of burials and extend the life of the cemetery grounds.

1,000-YEAR-OLD CHURCH MYSTERY CRACKED BY STUDENTS FROM KING CHARLES' ALMA MATER

Stewart told Fox News Digital the unadvertised cemetery is not easy to find — and he intends to keep it that way.

"I don’t advertise the cemetery, it’s all word of mouth," he said. "I don’t want to speed up the process. The cemetery right now is set up in a way that it’s going to last way in excess of 200 years."

Stewart, who has been part of the cemetery for nearly his entire life, said he spends about two hours each day sitting in a lawn chair among the headstones, surrounded by the animals he believes "never die" — and keeping watch over Liberty.
